extracted.intended_audience: students, historians, and practitioners interested in the history and practice of advertising (particularly street and general advertising)
extracted.subtask_description: A historical account of street and general advertising practices, media, and ethics, tracing developments from ancient signboards and criers to modern hoardings, billposters, and promotional stunts. Emphasises practical lessons about placement, presentation, medium selection, and public reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match advertisements to a paper's pretensions/audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements should be classed according to the pretensions of the papers or the cause they adopt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the weekly press vs provincial press distinction: choose publications whose editorial stance and readership align with the advertiser's message and social pretensions so that ads are appropriate to audience expectations and likely to resonate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use distinctive signs and pictorial tokens when literacy is low
rubrics_metrics.description: Where reading is scarce, advertise by rebuses or pictorial objects (e.g., a hare and a bottle for 'Harebottle').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, shop-owners used animals, tools, dress items, and pictorial rebuses to identify premises. When customers cannot read names, a clear visual token or rebus aids recommendation and word-of-mouth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt new and varied subjects as sign density grows
rubrics_metrics.description: As the number of signs increased, new subjects were continually required to attract attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repeated or hackneyed motifs; innovate in imagery and subject matter to stand out among many competing signs. Repetition by a small number of painters led to frequent duplication, so seek originality (colour, subject) to differentiate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer regulated posting (contractors/advertisement stations) over predatory billsticking
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisement contractors who purchased exclusive rights to hoardings provide dependable publicity compared with roaming billstickers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractors created orderly, regulated 'advertisement stations' unlike earlier billposters who pasted anywhere and often defaced others' work. Use organised contractors and legal stations for consistent exposure and reduced vandalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect property and avoid pasting on private walls or doors
rubrics_metrics.description: Billstickers who disregarded privacy and pasted on private walls, dwelling-houses, and street doors were a public nuisance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: indiscriminate pasting reduces public goodwill and intelligibility. Seek authorised, non-intrusive sites rather than defacing private property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select unobstructed, high-vantage locations (business thoroughfares, railway stations, blank walls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any one having a vacant space in a business thoroughfare and free from obstruction may do advantageous business with an advertisement contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose visible, unobstructed surfaces (station walls, sides of lines, house sides in busy streets). Vantage and freedom from obstructions materially affect an ad's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid promoters monopolising ad-space in a medium
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The very worst sign one can have as to the success of a medium is that of an advertisement emanating from the promoters or proprietors’ of that medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proprietors fill their own medium with self-promotion, it signals a lack of external advertiser demand and undermines perceived effectiveness. A healthy medium shows diverse independent advertisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match medium to audience literacy and media development
rubrics_metrics.description: Posters and handbills became useful only when printing and reading became general; earlier, criers and signs served the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select communication forms appropriate to the public's literacy and familiarity: oral criers or pictorial signs for low-literacy audiences; printed bills/posters when reading is widespread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure quality of oral delivery and presentation for public criers
rubrics_metrics.description: Greeks required a musician to accompany public criers to secure proper pitch and expression; presentation affects reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral announcements benefit from attention to tone, rhythm, and delivery; invest in presentation (voice, timing, performance) to increase persuasion and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intrusive or nuisance advertising techniques (sidewalk stencilling, littering handbills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stencilling the flagstones started small but grew into a perfect nuisance and was suppressed by police and magistrates; handbills and labels (e.g., adhesive labels) can be intolerable if excessive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques that annoy the public or clutter public spaces risk legal suppression and public backlash. Consider community standards and legal limits before employing sidewalk stencils or mass-distributed adhesive labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise legibility and tasteful placement over illegible mass-posting
rubrics_metrics.description: Undertakers' persistent, numerous small pamphlets and tactics (including making bills illegible by blacking) reduced intelligibility and provoked legal action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass or aggressive posting that results in illegible or disrespectful displays harms reputation and effectiveness. Aim for clear, readable, and tastefully placed materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure promotional stunts suit the product and public taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty stunts (e.g., advertising umbrellas by painting them on skiff sails during a boat-race) attract attention but may fail if ill-suited to public taste or product durability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attention-grabbing innovations must connect plausibly to the product and audience; a spectacle alone does not guarantee sales or long-term success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scale and multi-format materials for major campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Large theatrical campaigns used millions of labels, millions of handbills, thousands of posters, cards, and window materials to saturate public attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For major public events or launches, coordinated high-volume, multi-format distribution (labels, posters, handbills, wrappers, cards) can achieve widespread awareness; plan logistics and audience reach accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid advertising practices that damage public property or currency
rubrics_metrics.description: Defacement of coinage (pence and halfpence) for advertising prompted Parliamentary intervention and replacement of coinage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods that materially damage public goods or currency provoke regulation and can backfire; avoid using or defacing communal objects for promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use trade symbols, tools, and name-puns on signs to aid recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificers used tools as signs over workshops; punning on names was common on signboards and tombstones — e.g., a pickaxe for a gravedigger, a pig for 'Porcula'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ visual metaphors, trade implements, or playful name-puns on signage to make business type and identity immediately recognizable and memorable.
